overview.text: An electric circuit is an interconnected path of conductors and components through which electric charge can move. When the path is complete, a source such as a battery provides electrical potential that drives current. A simple circuit might include wires, a switch and a lamp or resistor; more complex circuits combine many components. Opening a switch breaks the path and stops current from flowing through that route. Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to show components and their connections. Circuits are essential to electrical devices, from household lights to computers and phones, whose circuitry can be extraordinarily small.

key_facts.text: Current can flow when there is a complete path; opening a switch interrupts the path and stops current in that circuit.
Circuit diagrams use standard symbols for components and lines for connecting wires.
Conventional current is drawn from a battery’s positive terminal toward its negative terminal. In metal wires, electrons move in the opposite direction.
In a series circuit, components are connected one after another in the same branch; in the simple series circuit described by OpenStax, current is the same throughout.
A capacitor can store electric charge, a property used in many circuits.
